    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/crohnsdisease.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">Disease</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ileocolitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Inflammatory Bowel <span class="qt1">Disease</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Enteritis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Ileitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> is a chronic (long-lasting) <span class="qt1">disease</span> that causes inflammation in your digestive tract. It can affect any part of your digestive tract, which runs from your mouth to your anus. But it usually affects your small intestine and the beginning of your large intestine.</p><p><span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> is an inflammatory bowel <span class="qt1">disease</span> (IBD). Ulcerative colitis and microscopic colitis are other common types of IBD.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>?<p>The cause of <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> is unknown. Researchers think that an autoimmune reaction may be one cause. An autoimmune reaction happens when your immune system attacks healthy cells in your body. Genetics may also play a role, since <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> can run in families.</p><p>Stress and eating certain foods don't cause the <span class="qt1">disease</span>, but they can make your symptoms worse.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>?<p>There are certain factors that may raise your risk of <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>:</p><ul><li>Family history of the <span class="qt1">disease</span>. Having a parent, child, or sibling with the <span class="qt1">disease</span> puts you at higher risk.</li><li>Smoking. This may double your risk of developing <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>.</li><li>Certain medicines, such as antibiotics, birth-control pills, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin or ibuprofen. These may slightly increase your chance of developing <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s.</li><li>A high-fat diet. This may also slightly increase your risk of <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> can vary, depending where and how severe your inflammation is. The most common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Cramping and pain in your abdomen</li><li>Weight loss</li></ul><p>Some other possible symptoms are:</p><ul><li>Anemia, a condition in which you have fewer red blood cells than normal</li><li>Eye redness or pain</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Joint pain or soreness</li><li>Nausea or loss of appetite</li><li>Skin changes that involve red, tender bumps under the skin</li></ul><p>Stress and eating certain foods such as carbonated (fizzy) drinks and high-fiber foods may make some people's symptoms worse.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> cause?<p><span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> can cause other problems, including:</p><ul><li>Intestinal obstruction, a blockage in the intestine</li><li>Fistulas, abnormal connections between two parts inside of the body</li><li>Abscesses, pus-filled pockets of infection</li><li>Anal fissures, small tears in your anus that may cause itching, pain, or bleeding</li><li>Ulcers, open sores in your mouth, intestines, anus, or perineum</li><li>Malnutrition, when your body does not get the right amount of vitamins, minerals, and nutrients it needs</li><li>Inflammation in other areas of your body, such as your joints, eyes, and skin</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A family history</li><li>A physical exam, including:
	<ul><li>Checking for bloating in your abdomen.</li><li>Listening to sounds within your abdomen using a stethoscope.</li><li>Tapping on your abdomen to check for tenderness and pain and to see if your liver or spleen is abnormal or enlarged.</li></ul>
</li><li>Various tests, including:
	<ul><li>Blood and stool tests.</li><li>A colonoscopy.</li><li>An upper GI endoscopy, a procedure in which your provider uses a scope to look inside your mouth, esophagus, stomach, and small intestine.</li><li>Diagnostic imaging tests, such as a CT scan or an upper GI series. An upper GI series uses a special liquid called barium and x-rays. Drinking the barium will make your upper GI tract more visible on an x-ray.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>, but treatments can decrease inflammation in your intestines, relieve symptoms, and prevent complications. Treatments include medicines, bowel rest, and surgery. No single treatment works for everyone. You and your provider can work together to figure out which treatment is best for you:</p><ul><li>Medicines for <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s include various medicines that decrease the inflammation. Many of these medicines do this by reducing the activity of your immune system. Certain medicines can also help with symptoms or complications, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anti-diarrheal medicines. If your <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s causes an infection, you may need antibiotics.</li><li>Bowel rest involves drinking only certain liquids or not eating or drinking anything. This allows your intestines to rest. You may need to do this if your <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> symptoms are severe. You get your nutrients through drinking a liquid, a feeding tube, or an intravenous (IV) tube. You may need to do bowel rest in the hospital, or you may be able to do it at home. It will last for a few days or up to several weeks.</li><li>Surgery can treat complications and reduce symptoms when other treatments are not helping enough. The surgery will involve removing a damaged part of your digestive tract to treat:
	<ul><li>Fistulas</li><li>Bleeding that is life threatening</li><li>Intestinal obstructions</li><li>Side effects from medicines when they threaten your health</li><li>Symptoms when medicines do not improve your condition</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Changing your diet can help reduce symptoms. Your provider may recommend that you make changes to your diet, such as:</p><ul><li>Avoiding carbonated drinks</li><li>Avoiding popcorn, vegetable skins, nuts, and other high-fiber foods</li><li>Drinking more liquids</li><li>Eating smaller meals more often</li><li>Keeping a food diary to help identify foods that cause problems</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may ask you to go on a special diet, such as a diet that is:</p><ul><li>High calorie</li><li>Lactose free</li><li>Low fat</li><li>Low fiber</li><li>Low salt</li></ul><p>If you are not absorbing enough nutrients, you may need to take nutritional supplements and vitamins.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney <span class="qt1">Diseases</span></p></content>

      <content name="title">Small Intestine Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Intestinal <span class="qt1">Diseases</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your small intestine is the longest part of your digestive system - about twenty feet long!  It connects your stomach to your large intestine (or colon) and folds many times to fit inside your abdomen. Your small intestine does most of the digesting of the foods you eat.  It has three areas called the duodenum, the ileum, and the jejunum.</p><p>Problems with the small intestine can include:</p><ul><li>Bleeding</li><li>Celiac <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li><span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span></li><li>Infections</li><li>Intestinal cancer</li><li>Intestinal obstruction</li><li>Irritable bowel syndrome</li><li>Ulcers, such as peptic ulcer</li></ul><p>Treatment of disorders of the small intestine depends on the cause.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/fistulas.html">
      <content name="title">Fistulas</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A fistula is an abnormal connection between two parts inside of the body. Fistulas may develop between different organs, such as between the esophagus and the windpipe or the bowel and the vagina. They can also develop between two blood vessels, such as between an artery and a vein or between two arteries.</p><p>Some people are born with a fistula. Other common causes of fistulas include:</p><ul><li>Complications from surgery</li><li>Injury</li><li>Infection</li><li><span class="qt1">Diseases</span>, such as <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span> or ulcerative colitis</li></ul><p>Treatment depends on the cause of the fistula, where it is, and how bad it is. Some fistulas will close on their own. In some cases, you may need antibiotics and/or surgery.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/iron.html">
      <content name="title">Iron</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ferritin</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is iron?<p>Iron is a mineral that our bodies need for growth and development. Your body uses iron to make hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells. Hemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. Iron is also important for healthy muscles, bone marrow, and organ function. Your body also needs iron to make some hormones.</p>How do you get iron?<p>Iron is found naturally in many foods and is added to some fortified food products. Foods that are high in iron include:</p><ul><li>Lean meat, seafood, and poultry</li><li>Iron-fortified breakfast cereals and breads</li><li>White beans, lentils, spinach, kidney beans, and peas</li><li>Nuts and some dried fruits, such as raisins</li></ul><p>Iron is available in supplements, either on its own or as part of many multivitamin/mineral supplements.</p>What causes low iron?<p>Most people in the United States get enough iron. The amount that you need each day depends on your age, your sex, and whether you consume a mostly plant-based diet.</p><p>Sometimes people can have trouble getting enough iron. There can be many causes, including blood loss, a poor diet, or a problem absorbing enough iron from foods. Those who are more likely to have low iron include people who:</p><ul><li>Have heavy periods</li><li>Are pregnant or breastfeeding</li><li>Are infants (especially if they were born premature or low birth weight)</li><li>Are frequent blood donors</li><li>Have cancer, certain digestive <span class="qt1">diseases</span>, or heart failure</li><li>Are on kidney dialysis</li><li>Have trouble absorbing iron because they:
  <ul><li>Have a digestive condition such as celiac <span class="qt1">disease</span>, ulcerative colitis, <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>, or Helicobacter pylori infection</li><li>Had weight loss surgery</li></ul>
</li></ul>What happens if you don't get enough iron?<p>If you have too little iron, you may develop iron-deficiency anemia. It may not cause symptoms at first, but over time, it can cause fatigue, shortness of breath, and trouble with memory and concentration. Treatment for low iron and iron-deficiency anemia is usually with iron supplements.</p>What happens if you get too much iron?<p>Too much iron can damage your body. For example, if you are healthy and take too many iron supplements, you may have symptoms such as constipation, nausea and vomiting, abdominal (belly) pain, and diarrhea. Higher iron levels can cause ulcers. Extremely high levels can lead to organ damage, coma, and death.</p><p>A <span class="qt1">disease</span> called hemochromatosis can cause too much iron to build up in the body. Hemochromatosis is inherited (passed down through families). It is usually treated by removing blood (and iron) from your body on a regular basis.</p><p>NIH: National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/vitamina.html">
      <content name="title">Vitamin A</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Retinol</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Vitamins are substances that your body needs to grow and develop normally. Vitamin A plays a role in your:</p><ul><li>Vision</li><li>Bone growth</li><li>Reproduction</li><li>Cell functions</li><li>Immune system</li></ul><p>Vitamin A is an antioxidant. It can come from plant or animal sources.  Plant sources include colorful fruits and vegetables.  Animal sources include liver and whole milk.  Vitamin A is also added to foods like cereals.</p><p>Vegetarians, young children, and alcoholics may need extra Vitamin A. You might also need more if you have certain conditions, such as liver <span class="qt1">diseases</span>, cystic fibrosis, and <span class="qt0">Crohn</span>'s <span class="qt1">disease</span>.  Check with your health care provider to see if you need to take vitamin A supplements.</p><p>NIH: National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements</p></content>
